::: {.lead}
The online races of *Pocket Quest* need servers: for the races, for the
leaderboard, for the saved progress of every player. Byte Bay could buy
servers and put them in a cupboard of the office. But on launch day ten
times more players come than on a normal day, and at night almost nobody
plays. In lecture 9 you saw how devices reach a server over the Internet.
In this lesson you learn where such servers live today: in the **cloud**.
You learn its kinds and service models, the cloud services that a game
uses, and how the cloud grows with the players, with its risks. Every
section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary cloud-computing data-centre cloud-region virtual-machine iaas paas saas baas public-cloud hybrid-cloud cloud-save cdn dedicated-server scalability >}}

## 10.1 What is the cloud?

The cloud is not in the sky: it is other people's computers, in big
buildings, rented over the Internet (@fig-own). Who shares these computers
gives three kinds of cloud (@fig-deploy).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 10.1 — Cloud computing and its kinds"}
**Cloud computing** means using computing power, storage and software from
a provider over the Internet, **when you need it**, and paying for what you
use (**pay-as-you-go**). The provider runs **data centres** with thousands
of servers in **regions** around the world. One real server runs many
**virtual machines**.

- **Public cloud:** a provider sells services to many customers.
- **Private cloud:** cloud technology for one organization only.
- **Hybrid cloud:** own servers or a private cloud together with a public
  cloud.
:::

![Own servers or the cloud.](images/own-or-cloud.png){#fig-own width=94%}

![Public, private and hybrid cloud.](images/deployment.png){#fig-deploy width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.1 — Two ways to run the races"}
1. **Own servers:** Byte Bay buys 10 servers for the launch peak. They cost
   money every day, also at night, and a broken disk is Byte Bay's problem.
2. **Cloud:** Byte Bay rents race servers by the hour, in a region near its
   players, and gives them back when the players leave.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.2 — Three kinds"}
1. A student team runs the server of its game-jam game in a **public
   cloud**: no hardware, and it starts in minutes.
2. A phone company that sells games keeps its customer data in a **private
   cloud**, for its own use only.
3. A studio renders trailers on its own PCs and adds public-cloud machines
   for one big trailer a year: a **hybrid cloud**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"The cloud is free and always online." Cloud services cost money per use,
and providers also have outages. Plan for both.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Choose the kind"}
Which kind of cloud fits? (a) a club with no money for servers; (b) a
ministry that must keep its data on its own servers, inside the country;
(c) a shop that runs its cash registers on a server in the shop, and its
online store on rented cloud servers.

*Your result:* three answers.

::: {.check}
(a) **Public cloud**: rent what you need, no servers to buy. (b) **Private
cloud**: only for one organization, on its own servers. (c) **Hybrid
cloud**: own servers and a public cloud together.
:::
:::

## 10.2 Service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and BaaS

The service models differ in **who manages what** (@fig-models).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 10.2 — The service models"}
- **IaaS** (Infrastructure as a Service): you rent virtual machines,
  storage and networks; you manage the operating system and the software.
- **PaaS** (Platform as a Service): you upload your code and data; the
  provider runs the operating system and the runtime.
- **SaaS** (Software as a Service): you use a finished application, for
  example an online office suite.
- **BaaS** (Backend as a Service): ready services for apps and games, such
  as player accounts, cloud saves and leaderboards, used through an SDK.
:::

![Who manages what in each model.](images/service-models.png){#fig-models width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.3 — Four ways to run the friends list of Star Garden"}
1. **IaaS:** a rented virtual machine; the team installs the OS updates, the
   database and the code.
2. **PaaS:** the team uploads only the friends-list code; the platform runs
   it.
3. **BaaS:** the game uses the friends service of a game back end; no server
   code at all.
4. **SaaS:** the team itself plans its work on an online project board.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/cloud-stack.html" poster="sims/cloud-stack.png" title="Cloud Stack: who manages what?" height="680" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that with SaaS or BaaS the studio has no responsibility. It still
decides which player data it stores, who can see it, and how long it keeps
it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Who manages it?"}
1. In **Cloud Stack**, set the layers right for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
2. For each, write one thing that Byte Bay still manages.

*Your result:* three correct stacks and three sentences.

::: {.check}
IaaS: the provider manages the building and the servers up to the virtual
machines; Byte Bay manages the OS, the runtime, the app and the data. PaaS:
the provider also runs the OS and the runtime; Byte Bay manages the app and
the data. SaaS: the provider runs everything; Byte Bay still manages its
data (who sees it, how long it is kept).
:::
:::

## 10.3 The cloud services of a game

An online game uses several cloud services at once (@fig-gamecloud). Each
one solves one problem of the players.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 10.3 — The cloud services of a game"}
- **Back-end services (BaaS):** player accounts, **cloud saves** (the
  progress of each player on a server, loaded after a login on any
  device), leaderboards.
- **Object storage and a CDN:** files that players download, such as new
  levels. A **CDN** keeps copies of the files on servers near the players
  (@fig-cdn).
- **Dedicated game servers:** they run the live matches, in regions near
  the players, and decide what really happens.
:::

![The cloud services of an online game.](images/game-cloud.png){#fig-gamecloud width=94%}

![A CDN: copies of the files near the players.](images/cdn.png){#fig-cdn width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.4 — The cloud of Star Garden"}
1. Login and cloud save through a game back end: a player who changes phone
   continues in garden 5.
2. The flower pack (60 MB) in object storage, delivered by a CDN with a
   copy in the Middle East.
3. No live matches, so no dedicated game servers: the game stays cheaper.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Putting big level packs inside the app package. The download from the store
becomes huge, and every small change needs a new app version. Keep big,
changing content in object storage.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A map of services"}
Choose a mobile game you know with online features. Write which cloud
services it uses (back end, storage and CDN, game servers), and for what.

*Your result:* a map with at least three services.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "A football game: an account and a cloud save
(back end); new kits and stadiums downloaded (storage and a CDN); online
matches (dedicated game servers)." Check: three services, each with what
it does for the player.
:::
:::

## 10.4 Scaling, cost and risks

The biggest strength of the cloud is that it can grow and shrink with the
players (@fig-scale). It also has risks (@fig-pros).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 10.4 — Scalability, and the risks"}
**Scalability** is the ability to add or remove servers as the number of
users changes; **auto-scaling** does it by itself, by rules such as "add a
server when 80 % are busy". With pay-as-you-go, quiet hours cost less. The
risks: costs that grow with use, **outages** of the provider, **vendor
lock-in** (special services make moving hard), and data laws about where
player data may be stored.
:::

![Launch day with fixed servers and with auto-scaling.](images/scaling.png){#fig-scale width=94%}

![Benefits and risks.](images/cloud-pros-cons.png){#fig-pros width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.5 — Launch day"}
1. With 5 fixed servers, about 3,700 players cannot join at 19:00.
2. With 9 fixed servers, nobody is turned away, but most servers do nothing
   from midnight to noon.
3. With auto-scaling, the servers follow the players: nobody is turned away,
   and the day costs less than with 9 fixed servers.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/scale-sim.html" poster="sims/scale-sim.png" title="Launch Day Scaling: enough servers, not too many" height="680" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Auto-scaling with no upper limit and no budget alert. A bug or an attack
can start hundreds of servers. Set a maximum and a cost alarm.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Play the day"}
In **Launch Day Scaling**, find the smallest number of fixed servers that
turns nobody away, and compare its cost with auto-scaling.

*Your result:* a number, two costs and one sentence.

::: {.check}
9 fixed servers turn nobody away. Auto-scaling also turns nobody away and
costs less, because it uses few servers at night and many at 19:00. A good
sentence: "Auto-scaling follows the players, so we pay only for the servers
we need."
:::
:::

## Case study: Cloud Match

Byte Bay and its partners have six jobs: a race server that needs a special
OS setting; a small leaderboard program; shared documents for the team;
accounts, cloud saves and a leaderboard through an SDK; payment data of a
bank that must stay in its own data centre; and build PCs in the office with
extra cloud servers for launch peaks. The Game challenge of the interactive
lesson uses these jobs. In the mini-game below you match each job with the
right model or kind of cloud.

Mell and Grance, *The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing*, NIST Special
Publication 800-145 (2011). Erl, Mahmood and Puttini, *Cloud Computing:
Concepts, Technology & Architecture* (2013), Chapters 3–4.

## Exercises

1. Explain cloud computing in one sentence.
2. What is a virtual machine?
3. What is the difference between a public and a private cloud?
4. In IaaS, who installs the operating system updates?
5. In PaaS, what does the studio upload?
6. What does BaaS offer a game?
7. What does a cloud save do for a player who changes phone?
8. Why does a game use a CDN for its downloads?
9. What is auto-scaling?
10. Name two risks of the cloud.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Using computing power, storage and software from a provider over the
   Internet, when needed, and paying for the use.
2. A computer made in software on a real server.
3. A public cloud serves many customers; a private cloud serves one
   organization.
4. The customer (the studio).
5. Its code and data.
6. Ready services such as accounts, cloud saves and leaderboards.
7. After a login, the new phone loads the progress from the server.
8. The files come from a copy near the player: faster.
9. Adding and removing servers by itself when the load changes.
10. For example costs, outages, vendor lock-in, data laws.
:::
